md: Two traps in the convention. The 4th argument goes in `r10`, not `rcx` as in a normal C call, because the `syscall` instruction itself overwrites `rcx` with the return address. And after the call, `rcx` and `r11` are garbage from your point of view. Compilers know this; hand-written inline assembly must list them as clobbered.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
md: `munmap` can fail with `ENOMEM` even though it frees memory. mmap(2) explains why: unmapping a region in the middle of a mapping creates two smaller mappings, and that can exceed the per-process limit.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Why the average hides the requests users remember
md: Report latency as a distribution: several percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9) plus the maximum, not a mean. The mean blends a few terrible requests into many good ones and describes no actual user.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Signalling firewalls: message categories, home routing, monitoring
md: Signalling firewalls apply three ideas: some messages never belong on the interconnect, some may only come from the subscriber's home, and some must match where the subscriber actually is. Hiding the IMSI (home routing) makes the third kind much harder to abuse.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Salt Typhoon: espionage inside carrier networks (2024 to 2025)
md: Salt Typhoon worked through routers and management planes, not through exotic telecom protocols. Patch edge devices, keep management out of band, make a central copy the source of truth for configuration, and treat lawful-interception data as a prime target.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: *Present* and a missing end date are not the same thing. *Present* is an explicit claim of a current role. A blank end date may mean the person forgot to fill it in. Pick a convention, store which case occurred, and do not silently treat blanks as current.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
md: Repeated sampling scales **coverage** smoothly; selection without a reliable checker does not keep up. The useful question is never only how many samples, but how good is the verifier at the tail.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Sequential thinking lets later tokens build on earlier ones, which parallel sampling cannot. s1 found that majority voting over the base model could not catch up with the budget-forced fine-tuned model.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
md: Every number here is one group's runs at 760M parameters or less. A later public reimplementation (lesson 8) found the full model did not always beat its baselines, while the memory itself consistently helped over attention-only variants.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
md: Every modern malloc fast path is the same idea as the 2001 magazine layer: a small, private stack of free objects per thread or CPU, refilled and drained in batches from a locked shared layer, with sizing policies to cap the memory that sits idle.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
md: Measure a hunt programme by what it changes: detections created, gaps and vulnerabilities closed, techniques examined, and the dwell time of anything it finds. Intrusions found matter most when they happen, but a quarter without one is not a failed quarter if the organisation is harder to attack at the end of it.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Kill chain and ATT&CK as analytic frames
md: Use the kill chain to ask "where can we act against this adversary, and how many independent ways?" and ATT&CK to ask "which of their known behaviours can we see?". Both answer defender decisions, which is why they belong in intelligence products.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack surface: every door, window and vent
md: "Internal only" is not off the surface. An endpoint reachable only from inside the network is still reachable by anyone who gets inside: a phished employee, a compromised vendor login, a malicious insider. Count it, and protect it as if the network were hostile.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Third-party access is a trust boundary you do not fully control. Give each vendor the narrowest path, watch it closely, and assume the vendor's own computers may already be compromised.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A forecast is a prediction made at an origin $T$ using only data up to $T$, for a stated horizon $h$. Every evaluation in this course respects that constraint.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Reading an X.509 certificate field by field
md: Common misconception: "the CN must match the hostname". Modern clients ignore CN for name matching and check SAN only; a certificate with the right CN but no matching SAN entry fails in browsers and in Python's ssl module.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Your first kernel: program_id, offsets and masks
md: `tl.load` with a mask but no `other=` leaves masked lanes **undefined**. That is safe only if those lanes never feed a result. Any reduction (sum, max) over a masked block needs `other=` set to the operation's neutral value: the value that leaves the result unchanged, 0 for a sum (x + 0 = x) and minus infinity for a max (max(x, -inf) = x).

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses
md: Misconception: "lambda is just a weight, any value works." Text cross-entropy and noise MSE live on different scales, and lambda decides how the shared weights split their capacity. Transfusion used 5, BAGEL effectively 4 (0.25 CE + 1 MSE is a quarter of CE + 4 MSE). Change the noise parameterization or schedule and the right value moves.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
md: Build-time specialization = **pick components by configuration, link statically, let DCE and LTO remove the rest**. Reconfiguring means rebuilding.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
md: At hundreds of dimensions, a distance does about 0.5 to 0.75 FLOPs per byte of vector it reads. SIMD makes the arithmetic cheap; after that, the bytes you move (and the cache misses you take) decide the speed.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Batching queries: from memory-bound scans to matrix multiply
md: The norm expansion is not a free rewrite. For near-duplicates it can lose most of its precision in fp32 and even go negative. Use it to shortlist, and compute final distances directly when small gaps matter.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: When a write becomes searchable: refresh, replicas and consistency
md: An insert-then-search test that passes on a laptop can flake in production, where refreshes, segment optimization and replica lag stretch the gap. Make the test wait explicitly instead of sleeping for a guessed number of milliseconds.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Agent loops: multi-turn rollouts and tool calling in verl
md: A mask bug is silent. If tool tokens get mask 1, the loss pushes the policy to predict tool output, which it never chose, and advantages credit or blame the model for text it did not write. If a parser rewrites the assistant turn and the loop re-encodes text, the trained ids differ from the sampled ones. Log a few decoded trajectories with their masks (`trainer.rollout_data_dir`) before a long run.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
md: A video world model is three choices: how frames become latents (VQ tokens or continuous), how actions enter (logged, learned latent codes, or text), and how the next frame is sampled (masked token decoding or diffusion). All of them pay for autoregression with drift and finite memory, and they are judged on fidelity (FVD, human studies) and on control (delta PSNR).

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Case: the 2025 ESXi escape chain, VMSA-2025-0004
md: Escapes are chains: a device bug for code execution in the per-VM process, often a leak to make it reliable, then a sandbox or kernel bug to reach the host. Each link is a place to defend: fewer devices, a tight per-VM sandbox, and fast patching when a vendor says "exploited in the wild".

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
md: The longer sequence costs compute. Linear layers scale with token count, so 577 vs 197 tokens is about 2.9x more work per layer, while the attention score matrix grows with the square, about $(577/197)^2 \approx 8.6$x. Simplified: real step time also depends on kernels and memory traffic. Higher-resolution fine-tuning trades accuracy for a large jump in cost.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching
md: pi0 replaces "decode 7 tokens per step" with "run a 300M expert 10 times per chunk". Cost no longer grows with the number of action dimensions or the control rate, and the output is continuous.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
md: A backend is mostly a *declaration*: what it supports, plus two factories. Selection, batching, KV layout and CUDA graph capture are all driven by those declarations, so a backend never needs to know about the scheduler.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: FP8 KV caches inside the backends: scales, kernels, support
md: A backend handles FP8 in three places: it declares which FP8 dtypes it accepts, its cache write divides by the layer's scale and saturates, and its kernel multiplies by a descale (and, with FA3, takes an FP8 query). The scales belong to the layer, not the backend.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
md: Resolution is the main lever for reading text. Fixed-size models downscale, AnyRes adds tiles up to a grid limit, and dynamic-resolution models spend tokens in proportion to pixels. In every case more legible pixels means more visual tokens.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
md: The hierarchy is about deterministic wait-free algorithms. Herlihy notes that if the guarantee may be probabilistic (finite *expected* steps), the hierarchy collapses: randomized consensus from atomic registers exists. And a high consensus number says nothing about speed; it only says what is possible.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: RMSE rewards hedging. A smooth forecast that predicts the average of possible futures can beat a sharp, realistic one on RMSE while looking nothing like real weather. Read RMSE wins alongside ACC, spectra (how much variation a field has at each spatial scale; a blurry forecast is missing the small scales) or probabilistic scores.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Beyond port 443: what FTP, SMB, SNMP, LDAP and SMTP give away
md: Enumeration is asking questions a stranger should not get answers to. Use safe scripts, get written approval for intrusive ones, and pair every answer with its configuration fix: anonymous off, signing required, SNMPv3, VRFY disabled.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Case: Uber 2016, when a bug bounty was used to hide a breach
md: Authorisation is judged at the moment of access. A policy published afterwards, an NDA or a bounty payment cannot make earlier unauthorised access legal, for the person who took the data or for the company that tries to relabel it.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS: how a server opts in to cross-origin reads
md: CORS is enforced by **browsers**, about **reading**. It is not access control on your server. `curl` or a script outside a browser ignores it completely, and a simple request reaches your server even when the browser will later hide the response. Authentication and authorization still have to happen on the server for every request.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Accounts, groups and SIDs: how Windows names every identity
md: SIDs, not names, are what Windows checks. A renamed Administrator still has RID 500, and a deleted and re-created account gets a new SID, so it does not inherit the old account's permissions.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA2: from passphrase to PMK to the 4-way handshake
md: Messages 1 and 2 move the nonces; messages 3 and 4 deliver the group key and confirm the keys, which is also how the handshake protects against downgrades. The PMK itself never crosses the air, but everything else that goes into the PTK does.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app storage: secrets on disk and in the package
md: Obfuscating a hardcoded secret (splitting it, XORing it, hiding it in native code) only slows an analyst down; the app must reconstruct it to use it, so an attacker with the app can too. If a value must stay secret from users, it must not be in the app.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
md: The searching count throttles wakeups, and the barrier on both sides of it prevents lost ones. Remove the throttle and you get a thundering herd; remove the barrier and you get stranded tasks with idle cores.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy does not mean faster for every request. It removes per-byte work but adds per-call and per-page bookkeeping. For small messages the copy is cheap and the bookkeeping can cost more, as lesson 5 measures.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: NLI entailment: is the label a true statement about the text?
md: A multi_label score near 0.6 is not a 60% chance the label applies. It is the entailment share after throwing away the neutral mass, from a model trained on MNLI sentence pairs, not on your labels. Treat it as a ranking score and set thresholds on labeled data.
